items.title: Video tutorials

items.content:
**Q. How can I set it up to better see the Field Guide while I work?**
**A.** You can set up a side-by-side view of the project and the Field guide by doing the following:  
- Right-click on a guide and open in a new tab. 
- Drag that new tab away from the browser to a separate window. 
- Size the two windows to optimize the view.
Narrowing the width of the activity window can move the extra information under the slide image, making the slide image the full width of the window.

**Q. I see a large, dark shape in a cell. How can I tell if it's a Monocyte or a Lymphocyte?**
**A.** Monocytes are 2-3 times the size of the surrounding red blood cells, while Lymphocytes are only slightly larger than the red blood cells.

**Q. I see a few connected dark shapes in the cell. How can I tell if it's a Eosinophil or a Neutrophil?**
**A.** Neutrophils have a lighter cytoplasm (background), while the Eosinophils have tiny, dark granules that created a darker cytoplasm, especially along the edge of the cell.

**Q. What if I can't tell if something is a white blood cell or debris?**
**A.** Do your best to identify any white blood cells using the example images of white blood cells and debris in the Field Guide.

**Q. What if I know it's a white blood cell, but I'm unsure about the white blood cell type?**
**A.** Some white blood cells don't quite fit the typical description for their type. Please look closely at the guide to see which type it most closely matches and mark your best determination. Remember to look for a darker background and outline of an Eosinophil, which can otherwise look like a Neutrophil.

**Q. What if I don't see any white blood cells on an image?**
**A.** That is possible and there's no need to mark anything if there aren't any white blood cells, just click "Done" to move to the next image.
**Q. What if an image doesn't appear to have the red-ish or purple-ish staining that I usually see?**
**A.** Some slides have sections with poor staining, so the red blood cells look like pale ghosts. You should still be able to see the darker staining of the interior portions of the white blood cells. Slides from different years have different stains, so some images look more pink and others more purple.

**Q. Why are some images blurry or poorly stained?**
**A.** Choose the "Low Quality Image" option if at least half of the image is too blurry or has too much debris to see the WBCs well. The blood smears are performed in the field at Cayo Santiago, so the conditions aren't always ideal to make perfect blood slides. We are working on reimaging a few slides that were imaged at a lowed resolution and will replace them as we get them. Please just do your best.

----------
***Single Cell Workflows***
**Q. What if there's more than one WBC in the image?**
**A.** Focus on the WBC that is the closest to the center and identify that one. There will be another image with the other WBC closer to the center, so it won't be missed.

----------
***Larger Image Workflows (not single cell):***
**Q. How do I get rid of a mark I made by accident?**
**A.** Click on the X in the upper-right corner of the circle. (if you don't see the X, click on the mark to make it show up)

**Q. How do I move a mark?**
**A.** Position the mouse over the mark until you see the hand icon, then click and drag it where you want it to go.

**Q. What if a white blood cell is on the edge of the image?**
**A.** Only mark the cell if you can see at least half the cell and can tell what it is. Do your best to determine the cell type.

items.title: Reptile - Dichotomous Key

items.content:
• Activated Thrombocyte: A thrombocyte (platelet) that has changed shape or function, usually as part of the blood clotting process.
• Agranulocyte: A type of white blood cell that does not contain visible granules in its cytoplasm. Examples include lymphocytes and monocytes.
• Azurophil: A type of white blood cell, typically a monocyte or lymphocyte, containing azure granules.
• Azure Granule: A type of granule found in certain white blood cells, particularly in azurophils, that stains blue with Romanowsky-type stains.
• Basophil: A type of white blood cell that contains granules staining dark blue or purple with basic dyes. Basophils are involved in allergic responses.
• Basophilic Stippling: The appearance of small, blue-stained granules in red blood cells, typically indicating lead poisoning or other blood disorders.
• Binucleated: Describes a cell that contains two nuclei.
• Blood Smear: A thin layer of blood spread on a microscope slide and stained for examination. Used to study the number, size, and shape of blood cells.
• Blood Typing: The process of determining an individual's blood group (e.g., A, B, AB, O) based on the presence or absence of specific antigens on the surface of red blood cells.
• Burst Cell: A cell that has ruptured, often as a result of processing, and is no longer intact.
• Cell Fake: An artifact in blood samples that may resemble a real cell but is not one.
• Complete Blood Count (CBC): A blood test that measures the number and types of cells in the blood, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
• Crenation: The formation of abnormal notches or scallops on the edge of red blood cells, often due to osmotic changes.
• Cytoplasm: The gel-like substance inside a cell, surrounding the nucleus, where most cellular activities occur.
• Dichotomous Key: A tool that allows the identification of organisms or cells based on a series of choices that lead the user to the correct name.
• DNA Sequence: The specific order of nucleotides (A, T, C, G) in a DNA molecule, which determines genetic information.
• Eccentric: Describes a nucleus that is located off-center within a cell.
• Echinocytes: Red blood cells with spiky or irregular edges, often due to changes in the cell membrane.
• Eosinophil: A type of white blood cell containing granules that stain bright red or orange. Eosinophils are involved in combating parasitic infections and allergic reactions.
• Erythrocytes: Another name for red blood cells, responsible for carrying oxygen throughout the body.
• Genetic Testing: The process of analyzing DNA to identify changes in genes, chromosomes, or proteins, often to detect genetic disorders or to determine ancestry.
• Granulocyte: A type of white blood cell with visible granules in its cytoplasm, such as neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.
• Granules: Small particles within cells, often containing enzymes or other substances, visible when stained under a microscope.
• Heterophils: The equivalent of neutrophils in non-mammalian species, containing large, red-staining granules.
• Hypersegmentation: A condition where a cell's nucleus has more lobes than usual, often seen in neutrophils during certain blood disorders.
• Lobe: A rounded projection or division of the nucleus in a cell, commonly seen in white blood cells like neutrophils.
• Lymphocyte: A type of white blood cell involved in the immune response, often associated with the production of antibodies.
• Lysed Cell: A cell that has been broken down or destroyed, the cell wall or membrane often having been ruptured by osmotic pressure or chemical processes.
• Mitosis (Mitotic Figure): A cell in the process of division, particularly during mitosis, where chromosomes are visible and being separated into daughter cells.
• Monocyte: A type of large white blood cell that can differentiate into macrophages or dendritic cells, playing a role in the immune response.
• Neutrophil: A type of white blood cell that is the first to respond to infections, characterized by its multilobed nucleus and fine granules.
• Nucleus: The central structure within a cell that contains DNA and controls cellular activities.
• Parasite: An organism that lives in or on another organism (the host), often causing harm. Examples in blood include Plasmodium, Trypanosoma, and Hepatozoon.
• Plasmodium: A genus of parasites that causes malaria, detectable in blood smears by the presence of its developmental stages within red blood cells.
• Platelet: Also known as a thrombocyte, a small blood cell involved in clotting to prevent bleeding.
• Polychromatophils: Immature red blood cells that are slightly larger and more purple-stained due to the presence of RNA.
• Proerythroblast: An immature precursor cell that eventually develops into a red blood cell.
• Reactive Monocyte: A monocyte that shows signs of activation, often in response to infection or inflammation.
• Red Blood Cell (RBC): A blood cell responsible for carrying oxygen from the lungs to the body and carbon dioxide back to the lungs for exhalation.
• Red Blood Cell Count (RBC Count): A measurement of the number of red blood cells in a given volume of blood.
• Segmentation: The division of the nucleus into distinct lobes, particularly in neutrophils.
• Slide: A flat piece of glass used to hold a sample of blood or other material for microscopic examination.
• Species: A group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, used here to refer to different kinds of animals whose blood is being analyzed.
• Stain: A chemical used to color cells or tissues so that they can be seen more clearly under a microscope.
• Thrombocyte: Also known as a platelet, a small cell fragment involved in blood clotting.
• Toxic Heterophil: A heterophil showing abnormal granules or vacuoles, often associated with bacterial infections.
• Trypanosoma: A genus of parasitic protozoa, some of which cause diseases like sleeping sickness, detectable in blood smears by their elongated shape.
• Vacuoles: Small cavities within the cytoplasm of a cell that can contain fluid, waste products, or other materials.
• White Blood Cell (WBC): A type of blood cell that is part of the immune system, helping the body fight infection and disease.
• White Blood Cell Count (WBC Count): A measurement of the number of white blood cells in a given volume of blood.
• Whole Blood: Blood that has not been separated into its individual components, containing red cells, white cells, platelets, and plasma.
